attribution_finding: Dennis p.510 is Vinson plurality quoting and adopting Learned Hand's formulation, not a single majority-authored passage. Brandenburg is per curiam; Cohen is majority.
fidelity_finding: Dennis and Brandenburg words correspond. Cohen strings genuine fragments in a different order: the taste/style conclusion follows the vulgarity sentence in the source, but precedes it here; 'It is largely because' omits 'Indeed, we think' without brackets.
pinpoint_finding: Cohen powerful-medicine passage starts at 24, outside cited 25–26; remaining taste/vulgarity words at 25. Dennis 510 and Brandenburg 447 correct.
scope_and_cutoff_finding: Historical trajectory must preserve imminent-directed-and-likely conditions, not create a categorical immunity for every speech category. Additional Yates/Sullivan sources not independently disposed here.
proposed_action_not_applied: Label Dennis plurality and nested Hand quotation; restore source sequence or label Cohen as a paraphrase; include p.24.
prior_repair_status: No repair performed in this audit

ledger_excerpt:
From Dennis v. United States, 341 U.S. 494, 510 (1951):
"In each case [courts] must ask whether the gravity of the 'evil,' discounted by its improbability, justifies such invasion of free speech as is necessary to avoid the danger."
From Brandenburg v. Ohio, 395 U.S. 444, 447 (1969):
"The constitutional guarantees of free speech and free press do not permit a State to forbid or proscribe advocacy of the use of force or of law violation except where such advocacy is directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action and is likely to incite or produce such action."
From Cohen v. California, 403 U.S. 15, 25–26 (1971):
"The constitutional right of free expression is powerful medicine in a society as diverse and populous as ours... It is largely because governmental officials cannot make principled distinctions in this area that the Constitution leaves matters of taste and style so largely to the individual. Surely the State has no right to cleanse public debate to the point where it is grammatically palatable to the most squeamish among us... [O]ne man's vulgarity is another's lyric."
